\chapter{Sixth to Tenth}
\label{ch:hi-ordinals-to-tenth}
\hlchaptermodality{83}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count in order all the way to tenth in Hindi, and say why chhatha is the one number the rule does not reach.}

The tenth closes the series and carries the ending past ten, so there is no second list to learn.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[chaṭhā / chaṭhī]{\hi{छठा} (chaṭhā) — the one hole in the rule}

\label{lesson:HI-C76-sixth}



\begin{quote}
Recalls open the chapter, at the four measured distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pā̃cvā̃} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pahlā} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kyoṁ} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{gāṛī} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mausam} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{subah} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{छठा}}
\textbf{\hi{छठा}} (\emph{chaṭhā}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{sixth}\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\hi{छठा} \hi{दिन}} (\emph{chaṭhā din}), \textbf{\hi{छठी} \hi{किताब}} (\emph{chaṭhī kitāb}).

The last lesson gave you a rule one lesson ago and this is where it fails. \textbf{\hi{छह}} is six, and the sixth is \textbf{not} \emph{chhahvā̃}. It is \textbf{\hi{छठा}} (\emph{chaṭhā}), with a retroflex \textbf{\hi{ठ}} that comes from nowhere in the cardinal.

\begin{cousinweb}
Sanskrit had \textbf{\hi{षष्ठ}} (\emph{ṣaṣṭha}) for sixth, and Hindi inherited it directly, worn down to \emph{chaṭhā}. It never went through the \emph{-\hi{वाँ}} machinery because it was already there when the machinery was built.

Which is the ordinary shape of this kind of hole: a rule spreads through a language and the words that are said most often resist it longest, because they are already known and nobody has to work them out. English does the same thing — \emph{went} is not \emph{goed} for exactly this reason.

So the ordinals are five inherited words and one ending: \emph{pahlā, dūsrā, tīsrā, cauthā, chaṭhā}, and \textbf{-\hi{वाँ}} for everything else. That is the whole system, and the rest of this chapter is the ending doing its work.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chaṭhā} — retroflex \emph{ṭh}
  \item not \emph{chhahvā̃} — the rule does not reach it
  \item the five that are words — \emph{pahlā, dūsrā, tīsrā, cauthā, chaṭhā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the sixth day. (\textbf{\hi{छठा}} (\emph{chaṭhā}) \textbf{\hi{दिन}}.) Why is it not \emph{chhahvā̃}? (\textbf{It was inherited whole} from Sanskrit \emph{ṣaṣṭha}, before the \emph{-\hi{वाँ}} rule existed.) And how many ordinals are separate words? (\textbf{Five}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sātvā̃ / sātvī̃]{\hi{सातवाँ} (sātvā̃) — seventh}

\label{lesson:HI-C76-seventh}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, then the seventh.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{chaṭhā} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dūsrā} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kyoṁki} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{rel} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{the letter dha} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{śām} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{सातवाँ}}
\textbf{\hi{सातवाँ}} (\emph{sātvā̃}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{seventh}\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\hi{सातवाँ} \hi{दिन}} (\emph{sātvā̃ din}), \textbf{\hi{सातवीं} \hi{किताब}} (\emph{sātvī̃ kitāb}).

\textbf{\hi{सात}} stands whole and \textbf{-\hi{वाँ}} goes on. After the hole at six the ending runs without interruption, and it will keep running for the rest of the number line.

Notice what you are now doing: you are not learning a word, you are applying something. Say \emph{sāt} and the seventh follows from it without a second act of memory. That is what a rule buys, and it is why the four irregular ones were worth meeting first — they were the price, and it has been paid.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sātvā̃}
  \item the rule — \emph{sāt} + \emph{-vā̃}
  \item \emph{sātvī̃ kitāb} — the seventh book
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the seventh day. (\textbf{\hi{सातवाँ}} (\emph{sātvā̃}) \textbf{\hi{दिन}}.) What happens to \emph{\hi{सात}} on the way? (\textbf{Nothing} — it stands whole.) And what changes for a feminine noun? (\textbf{\hi{सातवीं}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āṭhvā̃ / āṭhvī̃]{\hi{आठवाँ} (āṭhvā̃) — eighth}

\label{lesson:HI-C76-eighth}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, then the eighth.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sātvā̃} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{tīsrā} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kab} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sṭeśan} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{chhah, sāt, āṭh, nau, das} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dopahar} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{आठवाँ}}
\textbf{\hi{आठवाँ}} (\emph{āṭhvā̃}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{eighth}\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\hi{आठवाँ} \hi{दिन}} (\emph{āṭhvā̃ din}), \textbf{\hi{आठवीं} \hi{किताब}} (\emph{āṭhvī̃ kitāb}).

\textbf{\hi{आठ}} + \textbf{-\hi{वाँ}}. The retroflex \textbf{\hi{ठ}} of the cardinal is kept exactly as it is — the ending arrives after it and changes nothing on its way.

Hold \emph{chaṭhā} and \emph{āṭhvā̃} side by side and hear the difference. Both have a retroflex \textbf{\hi{ठ}}; in the sixth it belongs to the ordinal and not to the cardinal, and in the eighth it belongs to the cardinal and the ordinal borrowed nothing.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āṭhvā̃}
  \item the rule — \emph{āṭh} + \emph{-vā̃}
  \item \emph{āṭhvī̃ kitāb} — the eighth book
  \item \emph{chaṭhā} against \emph{āṭhvā̃} — one is a word, one is a sum
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the eighth day. (\textbf{\hi{आठवाँ}} (\emph{āṭhvā̃}) \textbf{\hi{दिन}}.) What happened to the \emph{ṭh} of \emph{āṭh}? (\textbf{Nothing} — the ending follows it.) What changes for a feminine noun? (\textbf{\hi{आठवीं}}.) And which of \emph{chaṭhā} and \emph{āṭhvā̃} had to be memorised? (\emph{\textbf{Chaṭhā}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nauvā̃]{\hi{नौवाँ} (nauvā̃) — ninth}

\label{lesson:HI-C76-ninth}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, then the ninth.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{āṭhvā̃} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{cauthā} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{the verb at the end} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ṭikaṭ} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{where chhah, nau and das came from} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{suprabhāt} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{नौवाँ}}
\textbf{\hi{नौवाँ}} (\emph{nauvā̃}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{ninth}\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\hi{नौवाँ} \hi{दिन}} (\emph{nauvā̃ din}), \textbf{\hi{नौवीं} \hi{किताब}} (\emph{nauvī̃ kitāb}).

\textbf{\hi{नौ}} ends in a vowel where \emph{sāt} and \emph{āṭh} ended in consonants, and \textbf{-\hi{वाँ}} attaches anyway. That is worth one sentence of attention: an ending that does not care what the word before it ends in is a \textbf{suffix}, not a reshaping — it is added, not fused.

Compare \emph{cauthā}, where \emph{cār} had to change shape to accept its ending. That is a fused form. This is not. Same language, two different ages of word-making, and you can hear which is which.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nauvā̃}
  \item the rule — \emph{nau} + \emph{-vā̃}, after a vowel
  \item \emph{cauthā} is fused; \emph{nauvā̃} is added
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the ninth day. (\textbf{\hi{नौवाँ} \hi{दिन}}.) What does \emph{\hi{नौ}} end in, and does the ending care? (\textbf{A vowel}, and \textbf{no}.) And which of \emph{cauthā} and \emph{nauvā̃} was fused rather than added? (\emph{\textbf{Cauthā}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dasvā̃]{\hi{दसवाँ} (dasvā̃) — tenth}

\label{lesson:HI-C76-tenth}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, then the tenth, which closes the series.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nauvā̃} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pā̃cvā̃} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ki} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{jānā} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{gyārah to bīs} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{śubh sandhyā} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{दसवाँ}}
\textbf{\hi{दसवाँ}} (\emph{dasvā̃}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{tenth}\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\hi{दसवाँ} \hi{दिन}} (\emph{dasvā̃ din}), \textbf{\hi{दसवीं} \hi{किताब}} (\emph{dasvī̃ kitāb}).

That is the ten. Say them in order — \emph{pahlā, dūsrā, tīsrā, cauthā, pā̃cvā̃, chaṭhā, sātvā̃, āṭhvā̃, nauvā̃, dasvā̃} — and count what you actually had to learn: \textbf{five words and one ending}.

And ten is not a boundary. \textbf{\hi{ग्यारहवाँ}} is eleventh, \textbf{\hi{बीसवाँ}} twentieth, \textbf{\hi{सौवाँ}} hundredth. There is no second list above ten and no third above a hundred; the ending you learned at five reaches every number you will ever say.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dasvā̃}
  \item the ten in order, \emph{pahlā} to \emph{dasvā̃}
  \item past ten — \emph{gyārahvā̃}, \emph{bīsvā̃}, \emph{sauvā̃}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the ten in order. (\emph{\textbf{Pahlā}} through \emph{\textbf{dasvā̃}}.) How much had to be learned as words? (\textbf{Five} — and one ending for the rest.) And say \textquotedblleft{}eleventh\textquotedblright{}. (\textbf{\hi{ग्यारहवाँ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
